A '''field''' is a [[set]] closed under two binary operations, with some special properties by definition.

It is a subclass of [[ring (mathematical concept)|rings]].

== Formal definition ==

Let $F:|F| \ge 2$ be a set, and $+_F,\cdot_F$ two [[binary operation|binary operations]] where

$$
+_F: F \times F \to F ,\, 
\cdot_F: F \times F \to F
$$

If $\forall a,b,c \in F$:

* $a+_Fb=b+_Fa;a \cdot_F b = b \cdot_F a$ ('''commutativity''')
* $(a+_Fb)+_Fc=a+_F(b+_Fc);(a \cdot_F b)\cdot_F c = a \cdot_F (b \cdot_F c)$ ('''associativity''')
* $\exists 0_F,1_F \in F: a+_F0_F=a, a \cdot_F 1_F=a$ ('''identity''')
* $\exists (-a) \in F: a +_F (-a)=0_F; \forall a \neq 0_F: \exists (a^{-1}) \in F, a\cdot_F (a^{-1})=1_F$ ('''inverse''')
* $a\cdot_F (b+_Fc)=a\cdot_F b +_F a\cdot_F c$ ('''distributivity''')

Then $(F,+_F,\cdot_F)$ is a '''field'''.

<blockquote>
Just like [[ring (mathematical concept)|rings]], $+_F,\cdot_F$ do not have to take the usual definitions of $+,\cdot $.
</blockquote>

<blockquote>
The smallest field is $(\{0_F,1_F\},+_F,\cdot_F)$.
</blockquote>

<blockquote>
Alternatively, a field can be defined as a [[ring (mathematical concept)|ring]] with additional properties:

* $a \cdot_F b = b \cdot_F a$ ('''multiplicative commutativity''')
* $\exists 1_F \in F: a \cdot_F 1_F=a$ ('''multiplicative identity''')
* $\forall a \neq 0_F: \exists (a^{-1}) \in F, a\cdot_F (a^{-1})=1_F$ ('''multiplicative inverse''')

Also, note unlike for [[ring (mathematical concept)|rings]], there is no need to specify distributivity for each slot. The slots for multiplication are symmetric in a field, because of multiplicative commutativity.
</blockquote>

<ref>{{#cite:Q2202}}</ref><ref>{{#cite:Q2204}}</ref>

== Examples ==

For each of the $F$ below, $(F,+_F,\cdot_F )$, where $+_F,\cdot_F=+,\cdot$ unless specified, is a field:

{| class="wikitable"
|-
! $F$
! Note
|-
|| $\mathbb{Q}$
| Rational number field, $1_F=1,0_F=0$
|-
|| $\mathbb{R}$
| Real number field, $1_F=1,0_F=0$
|-
| | $\{(a,b)|a,b \in \mathbb{R}\}$
| real 2D vector field, $1_F=(1,1),0_F=(0,0)$
|}

'''Counterexamples''':

{| class="wikitable"
|-
! $F$
! Why $(F,+_F,\cdot_F )$ is not a field?
|-
| $\mathbb{N}$
| $a=1 \in \mathbb{N}: \nexists (-1) \in \mathbb{N}$
|-
| $\mathbb{Z}$
| $a=2 \in \mathbb{N}: \nexists (2^{-1}) \in \mathbb{Z}$
|}

== Properties ==

=== $\exists ! 1_F,0_F$ (Uniqueness of identities) ===

{{Hidden proof}}
Suppose $\exists 1_F,1'_F$ two multiplicative identities

Then by definition $\forall a \in F$, $a\cdot 1_F = 1_F,\, a \cdot 1'_F = 1'_F$
Since $1_F \in F$, $1_F=1_F \cdot 1'_F=1'_F$

Suppose $\exists 0_F,0'_F$ two additive identities

Then by definition $\forall a \in F$, $a+0_F = 0_F,\, a+0'_F = a$
Since $0_F,0_F \in F$, $0'_F+0_F=0_F,\, 0_F+0'_F=0'_F$

By [[field (mathematical concept)#Formal_definition|commutativity of $+_F$]], $0'_F+0_F=0_F+0'_F$,

Hence $0_F=0'_F$.

Therefore both the additive and multiplicative identities must be unique.
{{End hidden}}

=== $\forall a \in F,\, \exists ! (-a)$ (Uniqueness of additive inverse) ===

{{Hidden proof}}
Suppose $\exists (-a),(-a)'$ two additive inverses of $a$, by definition

$$
a+(-a)'=0_F=a+(-a)
$$

Add $(-a)$ to both sides:

$$
a+(-a)'+(-a)=a+(-a)+(-a)
$$

By [[field (mathematical concept)#Formal_definition|commutativity and associativity of $+_F$]],

$$
(a+(-a))+(-a)'=(a+(-a))+(-a)
(-a)'=(-a)
$$

{{End hidden}}

==== $\forall a \in F,\, 0_F\cdot a =0_F $ ====

{{Hidden proof}}
By definition $0_F+0_F=0_F$, hence

$$
0_F\cdot a=(0_F+0_F)\cdot a=0_F\cdot a + 0_F \cdot a
$$

Add the additive inverse of $0_F \cdot a$, $(-0_F\cdot a)$ to both sides and by [[field (mathematical concept)#Formal_definition|associativity of $+_F$]]:

$$
0_F\cdot a+(-0_F \cdot a)=0_F\cdot a + (0_F \cdot a +(-0_F\cdot a))
0_F=0_F\cdot a
$$
{{End hidden}}

==== $\forall a \in F,\, (-1_F)\cdot a = (-a)$ ====

where $(-1_F)$ is the multiplicative inverse of $1_F$.

{{Hidden proof}}

$$
a+(-1_F)\cdot a= 1_F \cdot a+(-1_F)\cdot a= (1+(-1_F))\cdot a = 0_F \cdot a =0
$$
since [[field (mathematical concept)#$\forall_a_\in_F,\,_0_F\cdot_a_=0_F_$|$\forall a \in F,\, 0_F\cdot a =0_F$]].

Hence by [[field (mathematical concept)#Formal_definition|definition]], $(-1_F)\cdot a$ is the additive inverse of $a$

Since $(-a)$ is also the additive inverse of $a$, and [[field (mathematical concept)#(Uniqueness_of_additive_inverse)|the additive inverse is unique]], hence $(-1_F)\cdot a = (-a)$.
{{End hidden}}

==== $(-1_F)(-1_F)=1_F$ ====

where $(-1_F)$ is the additive inverse of $1_F$.

{{Hidden proof}}
$$
(-1_F)(-1_F)+(-1_F)=(-1_F)(-1_F)+(-1_F)(1_F)=(-1_F)((-1_F)+1_F))=0_F
$$

Hence $(-1_F)(-1_F)$ is an additive inverse of $(-1_F)$ by [[field (mathematical concept)#Formal_definition|definition]].

Since [[field (mathematical concept)#(Uniqueness_of_additive_inverse)|the additive inverse is unique]] and $1_F$ is the additive inverse of $(-1_F)$,

$$
(-1_F)(-1_F)=1_F.
$$

{{End hidden}}

==== $\forall a \in F,\, (-a)(-a)=a\cdot a$ ====

where $(-a)$ is the additive inverse of $a$.

{{Hidden proof}}
$$
(-a)\cdot(-a)=(-1_F\cdot a)\cdot(-1_F \cdot a)=((-1_F)(-1_F))\cdot(a\cdot a)= 1_F \cdot (a\cdot a)=a \cdot a
$$
by [[field (mathematical concept)#$\forall_a_\in_F,\,_(-1_F)\cdot_a_=_(-a)$|property]], [[field (mathematical concept)#Formal_definition|commutativity and associativity of $\cdot_F$]], and [[field (mathematical concept)#$(-1_F)(-1_F)=1_F$|property]].

Hence $(-1_F)(-1_F)$ is an additive inverse of $(-1_F)$ by [[field (mathematical concept)#Formal_definition|definition]].

Since [[field (mathematical concept)#(Uniqueness_of_additive_inverse)|the additive inverse is unique]] and $1_F$ is the additive inverse of $(-1_F)$,

$$
(-1_F)(-1_F)=1_F.
$$

{{End hidden}}

== Ordered field ==

Define [[binary operation]] $-_F: F \times F \to F$, s.t.

$$
\forall a,b \in F: a-_F b=a+_F(-b);
$$

define '''strict comparison operators'''  $>_F,<_F$, s.t.

$$
\forall a,b \in F: \\
a>_F b \iff a-_F b >_F 0_F\\
a<_F b \iff a-_F b <_F 0_F,
$$

by [[#formal definition|definition of a field]],

$$
\forall a,b \in F: \\
a=b \iff a-_F b =0_F \iff a \text{ is the additive inverse of } b.
$$

then define '''non-strict comparison operators''' $\ge_F,\le_F$, s.t.

$$
\forall a,b \in F: \\
a \ge_F b \iff a>_F b \lor a=b \\
a \le_F b \iff a<_F b \lor a=b.
$$

Then, a field $(F,+_F,\cdot_F)$ is said to be '''ordered''' if

$$
\exists P=\{x \in F|x>_F0_F\}: \\
\text{1. Closed under } +_F,\, \cdot_F, \\
\text{2. }\forall x \in F: x \in P \oplus x=0_F \oplus -x \in P.
$$

$P$ is then known as the '''positive cone''' of $F$.

=== Properties of an ordered field ===

==== $x>_F y \oplus x=_F y \oplus x<_F y$ (Trichotomy) ====

$\forall x,y \in F$.

{{Hidden proof}}
Let $z=x-_F y \in F$, by definition of an ordered field, $z \in P \oplus z=0_F \oplus -z \in P$

$$
\Rightarrow 
\begin{cases}
z>_F 0 \iff x>_F y \\
z=_F 0 \iff x=_F y \\
z<_F 0 \iff x<_F y
\end{cases}
$$

{{End hidden}}

==== $x>_F y \iff x+c>_F y+c$ (Compatibility over addition) ====

$\forall x,y,c \in F$.

{{Hidden proof}}
$$
\because x>_F y \\
\therefore x-_F y >_F 0_F \\
\therefore (x+c)-_F (y+c) >_F 0_F \\
\therefore x+c>y+c
$$

{{End hidden}}

==== $x>_F y \iff c\cdot x>_F c\cdot y$ (Compatibility over multiplication by positive) ====

$\forall x,y \in F,\, c \in P$.

{{Hidden proof}}
$$
\because x>_F y \\
\therefore x-_F y >_F 0_F
$$

Let $z=x-_F y$, by definition of the positive cone, $z \in P$

Since $c \in P$, by closeness of $\cdot_F$ over $P$, 

$$
c\cdot(x-_F y) \in P \iff c \cdot(x-_F y) > 0_F
$$

By [[field (mathematical concept)#Formal_definition|distributivity]] of field $F$,

$$
c\cdot x -_F c \cdot y= c \cdot(x-_F y) > 0_F
$$

By definition of the comparators,

$$
c\cdot x>_F c\cdot y
$$
{{End hidden}}

==== $x^2 >_F 0_F$ (Positive definiteness of square) ====

$\forall x \in F,\, x \ne 0_F$.

if $x^n$

$$
\char"5E: F \times \mathbb{N} \to F
$$
is defined as $x\cdot_F x \cdots \cdot_F x$ (product of $n$ $x$s)


{{Hidden proof}}
By definition of the positive cone, since $x \ne 0_F$

$$
x \in P \oplus -x \in P
$$

If $x \in P$:

$$
x^2=x \cdot_F x \in P
$$

since $P$ is closed under $\cdot_F$

If $-x \in P$:

$$
x^2=(-x) \cdot_F (-x) \in P
$$

since $P$ is closed under $\cdot_F$

{{End hidden}}
